extracted.intended_audience: state legislators, governors, and state agency officials (also local government, community-based organizations, businesses, and faith communities)
extracted.subtask_description: A policy guide that lays out six concrete steps and associated action options for state policymakers to promote responsible fatherhood, especially among low-income and noncustodial fathers. Includes core findings about fathers, attributes of successful programs, sample action steps, and state/community examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step One: Teach men to be good parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching young men to be responsible fathers involves teaching them to delay parenthood until they reach adulthood, are old enough to marry, and have the education and skills to support their children financially. It also means teaching all fathers — regardless of age, education, or income level — how to relate to their children in healthy and positive ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action Steps for State Officials (original wording where possible): Revise sex education curricula to include components on fathering and the responsibilities of fatherhood; require teens to study child health and child development in school; organize and fund fatherhood education and support groups linked to programs serving new mothers (such as WIC and Healthy Start); link paternity establishment programs to parenting programs for new fathers; support programs that work with incarcerated fathers to help them learn to stay connected with their children while in prison and be better parents when released. Examples & program models: MELD for Young Dads (10-book curriculum, local training and volunteer-led groups), Boot Camp for New Dads (pairing new fathers with veteran fathers). Recommendations: state education agencies should revise abstinence/sex education to include fathering; require young men study child health; fund father involvement programs linked to maternal services; link paternity establishment to parenting supports; support incarcerated-father programs. Program design notes: recruit in hospitals, schools, sports leagues; provide incentives such as free food, transportation, and child care; combine voluntary participation with mandatory referrals where appropriate; tailor curricula to cultural/language groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step Two: Help fathers improve relationships with their children's mothers
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve co-parenting, reduce conflict, promote healthy relationships, and where appropriate encourage marriage and two-parent family formation as strategies to improve child outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action Steps for State Officials: Encourage or require pre-marital counseling before couples can get marriage licenses; fund organizations that focus on culturally sensitive relationship counseling and/or model marriage; require fatherhood programs that receive state funds to train staff to spot domestic violence, report suspected abuse, and provide referrals to domestic violence services. Program guidance: offer conflict resolution services and co-parenting skills training; recognize that some parents pose danger and ensure programs have staff knowledgeable about recognizing signs of abuse and acting quickly to protect children and partners. Examples: Parents’ Fair Share curriculum for improving communications and conflict resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step Three: Remove barriers to work for low-income fathers
rubrics_metrics.description: Help low-income, non-custodial fathers find and keep steady, well-paid employment as a key strategy to increase father involvement and child support payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action Steps for State Officials: Link parenting programs for fathers to employment, education, and training programs; require state and local courts to refer men with child support arrearages to employment programs; require child-support enforcement offices to pursue modification orders for low-income fathers trying in good faith to find and keep a job; fund legal services to help fathers overcome barriers to employment (e.g., suspended driver’s licenses). Program examples: Fathers That Work (district attorney program with employer relationships), FATHER Project (case management, counseling, job training, placement, retention services, legal problem resolution), Workforce Investment Act demonstrations (use WIA funds for Responsible Teen Fathers Program). Problem framing: Many low-income noncustodial fathers face low education, lack of work experience, criminal records, suspended licenses, or child-support-related legal issues; programs must address these barriers comprehensively (case management + employer linkages + retention supports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step Four: Use federal funds to finance fathers' programs
rubrics_metrics.description: States should use flexible federal block grants and other federal funding streams to support programs for fathers, especially non-custodial parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and options: Use TANF block grant funds for activities meeting the four TANF purposes (ending welfare dependence, promoting employment, encouraging two-parent families, reducing out-of-wedlock pregnancies); set aside a percentage of TANF and Welfare-to-Work funds for programs serving low-income non-custodial parents; apply to the U.S. Department of Labor for a non-custodial parents demonstration project under the Workforce Investment Act; reserve TANF or Title IV-D bonuses to serve non-custodial parents; revise and simplify eligibility requirements for non-custodial parents to participate in TANF-funded programs; tap Social Services Block Grant, child support enforcement funds, Welfare-to-Work, and Workforce Investment Act funds. Examples: Long Beach uses WIA funds to support Responsible Teen Fathers Program; Georgia enrolls non-custodial fathers in state colleges/technical institutions for job training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step Five: Make the child support system work for families
rubrics_metrics.description: Change the child support system from punitive enforcement only to one that provides incentives and support so fathers can financially and emotionally support their children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action Steps for State Officials: Reinstate or strengthen state child support pass-throughs so at least some child support paid by low-income fathers goes directly to their families; forgive or decrease TANF-related child support debt owed to the state for fathers who participate in programs designed to increase earnings and improve parenting skills; rewrite state child support guidelines to allow self-support reserves for non-custodial working parents; amend state Earned Income Tax Credits to give fathers credit for child support they pay; invest in access and visitation programs to help fathers see their children. Problem framing & examples: Recognize average low-income fathers may have large arrearages often owed to states for welfare reimbursement; pass-throughs (e.g., Wisconsin) and debt forgiveness can incentivize payment; reframe enforcement to include positive incentives and services rather than only penalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step Six: Campaign to reinforce the message that 'fathers matter'
rubrics_metrics.description: Public awareness campaigns, agency audits, and community engagement can change social attitudes and fathers' own behaviors toward responsible fatherhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action Steps for State Officials: Create fatherhood commissions to advise governors and legislatures; initiate public awareness campaigns promoting responsible fatherhood; develop father resource centers as local clearing-houses for training and advice; conduct agency audits for father-friendliness; include a component on fathers in diversity training for public employees; convene fatherhood hearings or town hall meetings and invite fathers (including low-income non-custodial fathers) to speak. Campaign design notes: Tailor messages to target communities (avoid celebrity-focused ads if they don't resonate), use culturally specific materials (e.g., Spanish-language brochures), leverage community venues (e.g., barbershops), provide seed grants to community programs, and train social service providers in father-engagement and program evaluation. Example: Virginia Fatherhood Campaign used free airtime, billboards, barbershop campaign, seed grants, training, and community forums; evaluation found recall and behavior change in a survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Learning 1: Fathers care, even if caring is unconventional
rubrics_metrics.description: Fathers care, even if that caring is not shown in conventional ways — from emotional commitment to hands-on support and responsibility for child care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for policy: Do not rely on stereotypes of 'deadbeat dads'; program outreach and services should recognize diverse forms of father involvement and build on existing commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Learning 2: Father presence matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Father presence matters — in terms of economic well-being, social support, and child development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: Fathers' physical and emotional involvement yields measurable child benefits (better school outcomes, social skills, mental health), so policies should promote both financial and non-financial engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Learning 3: Joblessness impedes family formation and involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Joblessness is a major impediment to family formation and father involvement; lack of access to work pushes some fathers to evade support or work in the underground economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: Employment-focused interventions (training, placement, removing legal barriers) are central to increasing responsible fatherhood; treat employment access as a core program objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Learning 4: Current public approaches can create disincentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing approaches to public benefits, child support enforcement, and paternity establishment create obstacles and disincentives to father involvement; many view paternity and enforcement as punitive rather than supportive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: Redesign benefits and enforcement systems to reduce perverse incentives (e.g., pass-throughs, debt forgiveness, more supportive paternity services) and to build trust with fathers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Learning 5: Many parents need skill development to co-parent
rubrics_metrics.description: A growing number of young fathers and mothers need additional support to develop skills to share parenting responsibilities; many children are in 'fragile families' that need access to two parents committed to shared caregiving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program implication: Invest in relationship counseling, co-parenting curricula, and parenting education targeted to young/fragile families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Learning 6: Transition to committed parenting is developmental
rubrics_metrics.description: The transition from biological father to committed parent has significant developmental implications for young fathers; that transition is often incomplete and problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program implication: Design services that address developmental needs of young fathers (role models, hope-building, life-skills) rather than only financial obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core Learning 7: Intergenerational beliefs influence parenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Intergenerational beliefs and practices within families of origin significantly influence the behaviors of young parents; families often lack resources or desire to assist young men in becoming better parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program implication: Incorporate family-of-origin dynamics into program design and use mentoring/role-model strategies to counter negative intergenerational patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute 1: Focus on responsibility across life domains
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful programs 'focus on the need for young men to act responsibly in all aspects of their lives — not just when it comes to sex.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program design: Address school, relationships, and employment; help young men understand long-term consequences of teenage decisions and build agency/control over their lives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute 2: Set high expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should set high expectations for young men and not 'baby' them; ask whether participants are prepared to work and require readiness for full-time work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation: Combine support with accountability and clear expectations (e.g., readiness to work eight hours a day, five days a week); use curricula that challenge participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute 3: Separate curriculum for young men
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should have a separate curriculum and emphasis for young men because strategies that work for girls may not resonate with boys.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design guidance: Use male-oriented role models, culturally relevant references, competitive/team-based elements where appropriate, and curricula tailored to boys' developmental styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute 4: Give hope for the future
rubrics_metrics.description: Good pregnancy prevention and fatherhood programs give boys hope for the future and alternatives for proving manhood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program elements: Emphasize future-building (education, careers), create positive narratives and role models, provide tangible pathways (training, mentoring) that change perceived life trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute 5: Provide adult male role models
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful programs provide boys a close connection to an adult role model — preferably a man — especially in communities with high father absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation: Recruit, train, and retain male volunteers or veteran fathers to mentor participants; use peer-mentoring cycles (e.g., Boot Camp for New Dads "veteran fathers") and community-based recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute 6: Teach practical parenting and life skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should prepare young men to assume practical responsibilities of fatherhood (e.g., balancing a checkbook, childcare tasks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curriculum guidance: Include life-skills, money management, child care basics (diapering, feeding), legal issues (child support/custody), and employment-related skills so young men can evaluate readiness for fatherhood and perform caregiving roles competently.
